cues.text: Section ten is an applied lab on enterprise configuration management.
The LMS self-guided lab introduces FinTechNova, a hypothetical financial services organisation.
Its asset tracking is fragmented across locations in West Africa.
The objective for Session 01 is to create a central Configuration Management Database, or CMDB, and to enforce asset-registration policies.
Let us fix the key terms first.
A configuration item, or CI, is a managed component, such as a server, a database, an application or a network device.
A CMDB records configuration items, their attributes and the relationships between them.
An inventory tells you what exists.
A mature CMDB goes further: it also helps you identify dependencies and understand the effect of changes.
Next, shadow IT.
Shadow IT refers to technology adopted outside authorised oversight.
It creates unknown security exposure, duplicated expenditure and unclear ownership.
A central registry, together with automated policy checks, reduces these risks.
The lab itself uses Python and pandas in Google Colab.
Its registration function checks two things before adding an asset: whether the IP address is already recorded, and whether the region is authorised.
A compliant server in Enugu is accepted.
A proposed server in Nairobi, which uses an existing IP address, is rejected.
Note a weakness in the original lab: it tests both violations together, so the first rejection does not independently prove that the region rule works.
Here is a tutor-authored simplified example, with no dependencies.
We begin with a list called assets, holding one record: an asset with the ID DB-1, in the region Port Harcourt, with the IP address 192.168.1.11.
Then we define a set called approved, containing four regions: Port Harcourt, Accra, Kano and Enugu.
Now the function register, which takes an asset.
It applies three checks in order.
First, if any existing asset has the same ID, it returns "Rejected: duplicate ID".
Second, if any existing asset has the same IP address, it returns "Rejected: duplicate IP".
Third, if the asset's region is not in the approved set, it returns "Rejected: unauthorised region".
If all three checks pass, the asset is appended to the list and the function returns "Accepted".
The example then makes three calls and prints each result.
The first registers SRV-2, in Enugu, with IP 10.0.0.50.
The second registers SRV-3, in Kano, with IP 192.168.1.11.
The third registers SRV-4, in Nairobi, with IP 10.0.0.51.
The expected reasoning is this.
The first passes.
The second fails the duplicate-IP check.
The third independently fails the region check.
Only the first new item is added.
This is a teaching illustration, not an executed lab or a graded submission.
Now a real-world caveat.
Private IP addresses can legitimately repeat in isolated networks, so in production, uniqueness should be scoped to the relevant network or routing domain.
Also, a list or a dataframe is not a production CMDB.
And rejecting a record does not prevent an actual cloud deployment unless the gate is integrated into provisioning.
Production needs persistence, access control, audit trails, concurrency safeguards and reconciliation.
Finally, connect the lab to the principles.
Alignment is seen in the approved operating regions.
Risk is addressed by preventing conflicting configurations.
Resource management appears as asset visibility.
Value comes from less waste.
Measurement is about coverage and violations.
Connect it also to the management functions.
Planning is the policy.
Organising is the assignment of ownership.
Staffing is the choice of administrators.
Directing is driving adoption.
And controlling is the registration check itself.
